01

The problem: token spend

Every developer and every task adds to the bill. The two biggest levers -- which harness, which model -- get chosen on gut feel.

The problem

Agentic coding burns tokens at scale

Long-horizon, not one-shot

A task is tens to hundreds of LLM turns (~50-250, up to 300+), running 10 minutes to over an hour -- not a single prompt/response.

Prefill-heavy shape

Each turn replays a growing transcript as fresh input and emits a tiny edit. Real input:output runs ~150:1 to ~660:1 -- not the ~3:1 generic pricing assumes.

Cost hides in the choices

How many turns, how much context re-read, which harness, which model -- these swing the bill several-fold for similar quality.

Organizations are already at -- or heading toward -- trillions of tokens per month, and coding agents drive a large and growing share of it. That is the bill this repo helps control.

Public leaderboards can be saturated, and generic token pricing does not reflect this workload -- you need numbers on work that looks like yours.

Why it's different

Coding spend doesn't look like app traffic

Generic pricing and leaderboards don't tell you the bill. Only benchmarking on real tasks does.

The cost problem

Don't read the slide - point at the bars. Both are the same width. App traffic has a fat output slice (~3:1 input:output) - that's the ratio generic pricing and leaderboards assume.

Agentic coding is wildly input-heavy: real input:output runs ~150:1 up to ~660:1, because each of ~50-250 turns replays the growing transcript. The output slice basically disappears. It's frontier-model-driven and developer-controlled, and runs 10 minutes to an hour+.

If someone asks "isn't this prefill / cache-read?" - keep them separate. "Prefill" is just the model reading the input before it generates anything, so prefill-heavy = input-heavy (what the bar shows). That is not the same as cache-read tokens: caching is a pricing feature that bills the repeated part of the input cheaper instead of recomputing it. Because coding replays a huge, mostly-repeated transcript every turn, prompt caching is exactly the lever that makes it affordable - but "how much input" and "how cheaply that input is billed" are two different axes. We kept the jargon off the slide on purpose.

Two consequences to say out loud: for app traffic the lever is route & cache the premium slice; for coding the cost hides in the harness + model choice - which is why generic pricing tells you nothing and you have to benchmark on real tasks.

The cost problem

This is the picture behind the whole coding section. Two organizations doing the same kind of work, with completely different model mixes.

Left - Org A. Four models, and effectively all of them premium: opus-5 carrying 41% of token volume, opus-4-8 another 27%, gpt-5.6-sol 22%, and a thin 10% slice of haiku. Nothing routes down. Every task, however routine, gets a frontier model. This is the default state almost everywhere, because nobody ever made a decision - developers picked the best model they had access to and never revisited it.

Right - Org B. Same work, but roughly 70% of volume sits on open-weight models - qwen3.8-27b and kimi-k3 - served on their own hardware at a small fraction of the frontier per-token price. Premium is still there, at about 30%, and spread across two vendors (opus-5, sonnet-5, gpt-5.6-sol) rather than concentrated in one - reserved for the work that genuinely needs it.

The point to land: these are the same developers doing the same tasks. The difference is not talent or discipline, it is whether anyone measured which tasks actually require a frontier model. That measurement is exactly what the next few slides are about.

If asked "how do you know open-weight is good enough?" - that is the frontier chart, coming up shortly. Do not answer it here.

The frontier

This is the slide the whole coding section builds to.

1. Continuous, like evals. This isn't a one-time model pick. New models land basically every week, so the frontier moves. Re-running the benchmark is a habit - the same way teams already accept eval suites and CI. It's not a burden; it's how you stay current.

2. Model × Harness × Hosting - the "×" is the point. Cost and quality come from all three together, not the model alone. That's why a model provider can't just tell you the answer - they only own the model, not your harness or where you host it. You have to measure the combination on your own tasks.

3. What you get: a framework plus its open-source implementation. So this becomes a regular activity, and your developers work from a clear, approved model/harness guideline.

4. Where it's going - shift left. We shipped the "swe-router" skill (see docs/vision.md and issue #161) that pushes this frontier into your agentic-coding harness - regardless of which harness your devs use - so the right model/harness is selected automatically.

The one-liner: make it easy to do the right thing, by taking the model-and-harness decision off the individual developer.

Where the decision lives

Routing belongs where the context lives

Same word, two different jobs. At the gateway it is routing - a classification made on the prompt alone, which is right for application traffic. For coding the context is the repository, so the choice is decisioning: a judgement the harness can only form after it has looked around and asked. In effect the decision shifts left - out of the gateway and into the IDE, where the agentic coding harness already runs.

Follows from the input-heavy profile earlier: ~50-250 turns replaying a growing transcript, not a single self-contained request. Gateways still own the things that are stateless - rate limits, spend caps, policy.

The frontier

This answers the question a platform team always asks at this point: "we already have an LLM gateway - can't the router just live there?"

For application traffic, yes. The request is self-contained. The gateway sees one prompt, classifies it, and picks a model in milliseconds. Nothing else is needed, and that is the right place for it.

For agentic coding, no - and this follows directly from the input-heavy slide. The context is the entire repository. To know whether a task is a one-line fix or a refactor that touches twelve files, something has to open the repo, call tools, read code, and often ask the developer a clarifying question. That is a stateful judgement formed across many turns. A gateway sitting in the request path never sees any of it - by the time a prompt reaches the gateway, the decision has already had to be made.

So the naming matters: gateway-side it is routing; harness-side it is decisioning. Same intent, different amount of context required.

Land it as a shift-left move. The decision moves out of the central gateway and into the IDE, where the harness already sits next to the repo and the developer. The gateway keeps what genuinely is stateless - rate limits, spend caps, policy. That is exactly what the next slide implements.

Where it's going

Take the model choice off the developer

Task + repo → tier → frontier lookup → model · harness · effort. A swe-router skill triages the task, takes the cheapest model on the frontier that clears the bar, and escalates a tier if the result falls short.

Option 1 · start here · advise

Tell the developer, loudly

"For this task, switch to this model at this reasoning effort." The developer keeps their harness and can override it. No trust barrier - and every accepted call is evidence the routing works.

Option 2 · then · execute Next

Run it headless, hand back the result

The skill launches a headless instance of the chosen harness, at the chosen model and thinking effort, and completes the task. No manual switch, no decision left on the developer.

Sequence it: option 1, then option 2. Advisory mode earns the trust; move to headless once developers stop second-guessing the pick. Same frontier underneath - only the amount of automation changes.

Design: docs/vision.md · issue #161 - swe-router. Tiers: frontier / workhorse / budget, bounded escalation, every decision logged to routing.json.

The frontier

This is where the whole coding section lands. The frontier tells you which model to pick - but somebody still has to pick it, per task, and that somebody is currently a developer who would rather be writing code.

What the skill does: a router model reads the task and the repo and triages it into one of three tiers - frontier, workhorse or budget. It then consults the measured Pareto frontier and takes the cheapest non-dominated model that clears the bar for that tier. If the run fails or scores below expectation, it escalates one tier and re-runs, bounded by a maximum number of escalations. Every decision is written to routing.json, so the routing is auditable rather than magic.

Two ways to adopt it, and the order matters. Option one is advisory: the skill says loudly "switch to this model at this reasoning effort for this task," and the developer decides. Nothing is taken away from them, so there is no trust barrier - and each accepted recommendation is evidence that the routing works. Option two is autonomous: the skill spawns a headless instance of the chosen harness at the chosen model and thinking effort and just finishes the task.

Start with option one. Move to option two once developers have stopped second-guessing the pick. The frontier underneath is identical - the only thing that changes is how much of the decision the developer still carries.

Methodology deep-dive
04

Methodology

How a run works end to end, how cost is derived (GPU-seconds × $/second), and where models are strong or weak.

The approach

Two benchmarks, combined over real tasks

Quality

How well a model does a real coding task -- scored 0-100 by an independent LLM judge (codex exec, GPT-5.6-sol, high reasoning effort) against a fixed rubric.

Throughput → cost

Tokens/sec a self-hosted model sustains on a GPU, turning the instance's hourly price into a hardware-derived cost per task.

= Pareto frontier

Plot cost vs quality: the models where nothing else is both better and cheaper. That is the buying guide.

Crossing harnesses (Claude Code, pi, omp, kiro-cli) with models across three hosting paths gives real optionality -- the same model can be pricier under one agent yet cheaper and faster under another.

The method

What is a Pareto frontier?

The set of models where no other model is both higher-scoring AND cheaper. Those are the only models worth considering. Everything else is dominated -- some frontier model beats it on both axes, so there is never a reason to pick it.

On the frontier

Non-dominated: to do better you must pay more, and to pay less you must accept a lower score. The real trade-off curve.

Dominated (skip it)

Example from our data: kimi-k2.7-code (69.98, $3.13/task) is beaten by qwen3.8-27b (78.48, $1.47/task) -- higher score and lower cost (both self-hosted). kimi-k2.7-code is off the frontier.

How to read it

Pick the quality your task needs (y-axis), then take the leftmost model on the frontier at that level -- the cheapest way to buy that quality.

Cost bases differ (metered Bedrock vs hardware-derived self-hosted), so we also draw the frontier within each hosting basis.

Methodology · how a run works

From long-horizon task to a cost/quality point

1 · Long-horizon task

Point the agent at a real repo + issue. It drives an open-ended tool-use loop over ~50-250 turns (up to 300+), ~10 min to over an hour per task.

2 · Prefill-heavy tokens

Each turn replays the growing transcript as fresh input and emits a tiny edit -- ~150:1 to ~660:1 input:output. Measured, not assumed.

3 · Six artifacts

Lands github-issue, LLD, review, testing + the implemented change (patch.diff, implementation.md) on disk.

4 · Judge the quality

An independent judge (codex exec, GPT-5.6-sol, high effort) scores each artifact 0-100 on completeness, correctness, specificity, risk-awareness against a fixed rubric, read-only against a fresh clone.

5 · Marry with throughput

Multiply each run's real tokens by the model's measured tokens/sec on its GPU to get a hardware-derived cost per task -- quality × cost on the same real work.

= One frontier point

Every model becomes a (cost, quality) point; the non-dominated set is the frontier a buyer chooses from.

Cost basis

Two non-comparable cost bases

Metered (Bedrock)

A hosted API's real per-token bill, summed over the run. Benefits from prompt caching -- cache-read tokens billed at ~10%.

Hardware-derived (self-hosted)

A rented GPU has no per-token bill. Cost = GPU-seconds × $/second = (tokens ÷ measured throughput) × instance $/hr. Not wall-clock × $/hr -- that would charge idle agent-thinking time.

Compare within a hosting basis. Cross-hosting dollars are an order-of-magnitude result, not an exact tie -- each side credits prompt caching on its own terms.

Full cost methodology →

Self-hosted economics

What lowers self-hosted cost

Concurrency, up to the KV wall

Amortize the fixed $/hr across more sessions -- until the KV cache saturates. On a big model that wall comes early (GLM-5.2 saturates at ~c=5 on 8×H200).

Model-to-box fit

A small-active MoE that fits on half the box serves far more concurrent sessions per dollar than a model that fills it.

Reserved / committed pricing

The leaderboard prices both GPU families at their 3-year commitment rate (p5en.48xlarge $27.72/hr, g6e.12xlarge $4.53/hr, in pricing.json). On-demand is ~2.3x higher and a 1-year plan sits between -- each shifts the frontier, and cost is linear in $/hr.

Caching is already baked into the throughput (98-99% prefix-cache hit rate raises tokens/sec) -- so it shows up as a lower rate, not a separate discount. The lever is KV headroom, which trades against context window and therefore accuracy: no free lunch.

The harness moves both axes

So pick it per model

The same model lands in two different places under two harnesses. A harness is a cost lever the way a model is, and neither choice is safe to make once and forget.
